title: Futures, Forwards and Swaps
intro: A derivative is a contract whose value comes from something else: a stock index, an interest rate, a currency, a commodity. Futures, forwards and swaps are the simplest kind: agreements to exchange something at a set price in the future. They let companies and investors hedge risks, and let speculators take large positions with little money down. This page explains how they work and how they are priced.

blocks.text: A forward is a private agreement to buy or sell an asset on a future date at a price fixed today. A farmer can sell wheat forward to lock in a price for the harvest; an importer can buy dollars forward to fix the cost of goods ordered. No money changes hands until the delivery date, and each side bears the risk that the other won't pay.

A future is a standardized forward traded on an exchange (CME Group in Chicago, ICE, Eurex and others), with a clearinghouse in the middle of every trade, so neither side faces the other's credit risk. Each contract has a fixed size and date: one S&P 500 E-mini future covers \$50 times the index; one crude oil contract is 1,000 barrels. Most futures are closed before expiry rather than delivered.

To trade futures you post initial margin, typically a few percent to about 10% of the contract's value. Every day gains and losses are settled in cash (marking to market): if the price moves against you and your account falls below the maintenance margin, you must top it up at once (a variation margin call). This daily settlement is what makes futures safe for the clearinghouse and dangerous for an under-funded trader: a futures position is leverage, and a 5% move on a contract with 5% margin doubles or wipes out your stake.
You can get the asset in a year two ways: buy it today and hold it (paying the financing cost but collecting any income), or agree a forward price $F$ today. Arbitrage forces them to cost the same:

blocks.caption: Forward price on an asset with spot S, interest rate r, income yield q (dividends), time T in years.

items: Stock index futures: $q$ is the dividend yield. With rates above dividend yields the future trades above spot.
Currencies: $q$ is the foreign interest rate, which gives covered interest parity (see Parity, Carry and Hedging).

Commodities: add storage costs $u$ and subtract a convenience yield $y$, the benefit of having the physical good in hand: $F_0 = S_0 e^{(r + u - y)T}$. When inventories are scarce the convenience yield is high and the curve is in backwardation; when storage is plentiful it is in contango.
Bonds: Treasury futures deliver from a basket of bonds, with the cheapest to deliver setting the price.

blocks.text: The difference between spot and futures price is the basis. It shrinks to zero as the contract approaches expiry, because at expiry the future is the spot.

items: Hedging: an airline buys jet fuel futures to fix its fuel costs; a fund manager sells index futures to protect a portfolio for a few weeks without selling the stocks; a miner sells copper forward.
Cheap exposure: futures give market exposure without buying all the securities; institutions use them to equitize cash or shift asset allocation fast.
Speculation: a trend-following ('managed futures') fund goes long or short across dozens of futures markets. Such strategies made money in 2008 and 2022, when stocks and bonds struggled.
Price discovery: futures often trade around the clock and lead the cash market.

blocks.text: The hedge ratio that minimizes the variance of a hedged position is $h^* = \rho\,\sigma_S/\sigma_F$, where $\rho$ is the correlation between changes in the spot and futures prices. To hedge a stock portfolio with index futures, the number of contracts is about $\beta \times$ portfolio value / (futures price $\times$ contract multiplier).

A swap exchanges one stream of payments for another. The most common is the interest rate swap: one side pays a fixed rate, the other a floating rate (in the US now usually SOFR), on a notional amount that is never exchanged. A company with a floating-rate loan can swap to fixed to lock in its cost; a bank can do the opposite. The fixed swap rate is set so the swap is worth zero at the start, which makes it an average of expected future floating rates. The outstanding notional of interest rate derivatives is in the hundreds of trillions of dollars, though the amounts actually at risk are far smaller.

items: Currency swaps exchange principal and interest in two currencies.

Credit default swaps (CDS): the buyer pays a yearly premium; the seller pays the loss if a named borrower defaults. AIG's huge unhedged sales of CDS on mortgage securities nearly destroyed it in 2008.

Total return swaps pay the total return of an asset in exchange for a financing rate, giving exposure without ownership. Archegos Capital used them to build hidden leveraged positions and collapsed in 2021, costing its banks over \$10 billion.

blocks.text: Futures and swaps are zero-sum before costs: every dollar one side gains, the other loses. Their value to the economy is in moving risk to those willing to bear it, not in creating return. For an individual, their main dangers are leverage and margin calls.

blocks.title: Index future
blocks.text: An index is at 5,000, the one-year interest rate is 5% and the dividend yield is 1.5% (both continuous). What should the one-year future trade at?

blocks.title: Margin
blocks.text: You buy one E-mini S&P 500 future (\$50 × index) at 5,000 with initial margin of \$12,000. What is the position's value, your leverage, and your loss if the index falls 4%?
solution: A 4% fall is 200 points: $200 \times 50 = \$10{,}000$, more than 80% of your margin.
